stem: A client who recently started lamotrigine develops a new rash. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.A: Continue lamotrigine and report the rash only if blisters develop
options.B: Skip one dose, then restart at the same dose if the rash fades
options.C: Increase the dose more slowly while continuing the medication
options.D: Do not take another dose and contact the prescriber immediately for evaluation

rationale: Lamotrigine carries a boxed warning for life-threatening serious skin rashes, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. Because benign and serious rashes cannot reliably be distinguished at onset, the current label directs that lamotrigine be discontinued at the first sign of rash unless the rash is clearly not drug related. Therefore D is the safest instruction pending clinical evaluation. A and C continue exposure despite the warning, and B proposes an unsupervised restart that is not supported by the label.
educational_objective: Teach clients taking lamotrigine to stop the medication and promptly contact the prescriber when a new rash appears because early benign and life-threatening rashes cannot be reliably distinguished.

source_claim_supported: Lamotrigine can cause life-threatening serious rashes; it should be discontinued at the first sign of rash unless the rash is clearly not drug related, and restart after discontinuation for rash requires careful benefit-risk consideration.

correction_summary: Strengthened the action from generic 'contact the provider' to the exact label-supported instruction not to continue lamotrigine pending evaluation. Replaced the older 2025 FDA PDF citation with the current July 2026 DailyMed label and exact boxed-warning/§5.1 locators. Removed the unsupported blanket statement that every rash is Stevens-Johnson syndrome; the rationale instead reflects the label's inability to predict which early rash will become serious.
audit_findings: D is the only option consistent with the boxed warning. A and C continue drug exposure; B proposes an unsupervised restart. The item does not claim every rash is drug-related or life-threatening, but correctly applies the label's default discontinuation rule unless clearly non-drug-related. No second answer, cueing, unsupported precision, or unresolved conflict remains.
